title: What I look for on a first site walk
author: Elena Marlowe
summary: Before I draw anything, I walk a lot four times: morning, noon, evening, and after rain. Here is what I am actually looking for.
body:
Before I draw anything, I walk a lot four times: morning, noon, evening, and after rain. Here is what I am actually looking for.

Start with water

Where does rain go, and where does it want to stay? The answer decides foundations, floors and half the budget.

Find the shade at 6 pm

In Central Texas the west sun is the client. I mark where shade falls in August, not where it falls on the day we meet.

Listen

Roads, neighbors, birds. A courtyard can fix noise; a floor plan cannot fix a bad first decision about orientation.

title: ADUs in Austin: what fits, what the city asks, what it costs
author: Elena Marlowe
summary: Austin lets most single-family lots add a small second home. The rules are friendlier than they were — and still full of surprises.
body:
Austin lets most single-family lots add a small second home. The rules are friendlier than they were — and still full of surprises.

Size and height

Most lots allow up to about 1,100 square feet or a share of your lot, with height limits near neighbors. Heritage trees redraw everything.

What the city reviews

Site plan, tree protection, drainage and utilities. A survey and a tree survey save months.

What drives cost

Kitchens and baths, sewer connections, and whether the ADU shares the main house systems.

title: Remodel or rebuild? A honest way to decide
author: Elena Marlowe
summary: Sometimes the kindest thing an architect can say is: keep the house. Sometimes it is: stop spending on this one. Here is my test.
body:
Sometimes the kindest thing an architect can say is: keep the house. Sometimes it is: stop spending on this one. Here is my test.

Keep the bones honest

Good structure, a roof worth keeping, and a plan that is one or two walls from working — remodel.

Count what you cannot change

Ceiling height, orientation and lot coverage do not improve with new cabinets.

Price both, early

A rough price for each path, from a builder, before design goes far. Sentiment is allowed; surprises are not.

title: Designing for August: shade, breeze and limestone
author: Elena Marlowe
summary: Hill Country houses stayed cool long before air conditioning. The old tricks still work, and they make better rooms.
body:
Hill Country houses stayed cool long before air conditioning. The old tricks still work, and they make better rooms.

Shade before glass

Porches, deep overhangs and west walls with few, high windows. Glass belongs under shade.

Let air through

Windows on two sides of every room, high and low. A house that can breathe needs less help.

Mass where it helps

Stone and concrete floors even out the day, releasing the night's cool slowly.

title: How working with a solo architect actually works
author: Elena Marlowe
summary: One architect means no hand-offs and no layers. It also means I take few projects. Here is the rhythm, honestly.
body:
One architect means no hand-offs and no layers. It also means I take few projects. Here is the rhythm, honestly.

You get me

Every meeting, drawing and site visit. Questions go to the person who can answer them.

Fewer, slower, deeper

Four to six projects a year. If your timeline needs a big team, I will say so and name names.

Decisions in writing

Your portal holds every drawing, update and decision, so nothing lives only in a phone call.

title: Notes from site: a limestone wall, laid by hand
author: Elena Marlowe
summary: Watching masons lay a courtyard wall taught me more about detail drawings than a year of office work.
body:
Watching masons lay a courtyard wall taught me more about detail drawings than a year of office work.

Draw it like they build it

Every stone course in my drawings now matches how the crew actually lays it.

Leave room for hands

A detail that only works on paper will be fixed on site — by someone else, at your cost.

Go and watch

I schedule site days around the trades I most need to learn from. The house gets better; so do the drawings.
